steps.stepTitle: Scene 1: Broken Questions in the Interrogation Room
steps.settingDescription: Detective Ira is verifying witnesses' alibis after a missing ledger incident. Chikoo volunteers to read the suspect's questions—and mangles the auxiliaries!

dialogues.line: Aha! Did you saw anything? Didn't nobody open the cabinet? And why you were standing there, eh?!
Hold everything, Chikoo! You used 'saw' after 'Did', piled 'didn't' onto 'nobody', and forgot to invert 'were' before 'you'!

Negatives and Interrogatives follow crisp rules: bring in 'do/does/did' when no auxiliary is present (returning the main verb to base V1!), avoid double negatives, and invert the first auxiliary before the subject in questions.
Plus, watch out for subject Wh-questions ('Who locked the door?'—no 'did'!) and tricky Question Tags like 'I am right, aren't I?'

steps.storyCallout: Goal: Form accurate negatives and yes/no, wh-, and tag questions without double negatives or auxiliary slips.

steps.stepTitle: Discover: Forming Negatives & Avoiding Double Negatives
steps.memoryAidLabel: Memory Aid (Peculiar Definition — Not a Formal Rule)
steps.peculiarDefinition: 'Do / Does / Did' is the Emergency Generator for negatives and questions: whenever a sentence has ONLY a bare main verb ('She wrote', 'They play'), call in 'does/do/did' to hold 'not'—and strip '-s' or past tense off the main verb because the generator carries it now ('She didn't write', NEVER *didn't wrote)!
steps.formalDefinition: English negatives place 'not' (or 'n't') immediately after the first auxiliary verb (be, have, modal, or inserted do-support for simple present/past main verbs). Polarity items shift in negatives ('some → any', 'already → yet', 'too → either'), and standard English avoids stacking two negative words in the same clause.
steps.simpleExplanation:
Master three negative rules:
1) Existing Auxiliary vs. Do-Support: If 'am/is/are/was/were, have/has/had, can/will/must' is present, place 'not' right after the FIRST auxiliary ('She has not been waiting'). Otherwise, insert 'do not / does not / did not' + BARE V1 ('He does not play', 'They did not go'). Watch 'have' as a main verb of possession: 'She doesn't have a key' (or formal 'She hasn't a key'—never *She hasn't to do? Actually 'doesn't have to'!).
2) One Negative Only: Never combine 'not/n't' with 'nothing, nobody, nowhere, never, hardly, seldom, scarcely' (*I didn't tell nobody → 'I didn't tell anybody' OR 'I told nobody').
3) Polarity Shifts: In negative sentences, change 'some' → 'any' ('There isn't any milk'), 'already' → 'yet' ('He hasn't arrived yet'), and 'too' → 'either' ('I don't like bitter gourd either').

structurePatterns.formula: Simple Present: do / does + not + Bare V1 | Simple Past: did + not + Bare V1
structurePatterns.sample: Riya doesn't know (NOT *knows). / Kabir didn't break (NOT *broke) the lamp.

structurePatterns.formula: not + anything / anybody / anywhere / either  ≡  nothing / nobody / nowhere / neither
structurePatterns.sample: We didn't find anything. = We found nothing. (NEVER *didn't find nothing)

realLifeExamples.sentence: Detective Ira did not find any footprints near the window, and Vaani hadn't seen anyone either.
He rarely speaks during meetings, and neither of his partners knows the password.
realLifeExamples.contextNote: Semi-negative 'rarely' and 'neither' stay positive on the verb ('speaks', 'knows').

correctVsIncorrect.incorrectSentence: Chikoo didn't went to the vault, and he didn't tell nobody nothing!
correctVsIncorrect.correctSentence: Chikoo didn't go to the vault, and he didn't tell anybody anything!
correctVsIncorrect.whyItHappens: After 'didn't', return the verb to V1 ('go'), and use only one negative ('didn't... anybody anything' OR 'told nobody anything').

exceptions: When 'need' and 'dare' act as modals in negatives, use bare V1 ('You needn't hurry'); as ordinary main verbs, use do-support + 'to' ('You don't need to hurry').

steps.storyPrompt: Detective Ira spots two slips in Chikoo's interrogation transcript: "The suspect didn't wrote no message before midnight."
steps.questionPrompt: Pick the grammatically accurate negative sentence:
options: The suspect didn't write no message before midnight.
The suspect didn't wrote any message before midnight.
The suspect didn't write any message before midnight.
The suspect not wrote any message before midnight.
acceptedAnswers: The suspect didn't write any message before midnight.
steps.hint: After 'didn't', use base verb 'write' (not 'wrote'), and replace 'no' with 'any' so there is only ONE negative!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Detective Ira: "Transcript clean! 'Didn't write' uses V1, and 'any' keeps a single clear negative."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Use V1 ('write') after 'didn't', and change 'no message' to 'any message'.

feedbackWrongByOption.The suspect didn't write no message befo: Double negative! 'Didn't' + 'no' cancel awkwardly in standard English.

steps.simplerExample: He didn't buy any apples (OR: He bought no apples).

steps.storyPrompt: Vaani turns "Someone has already unlocked the safe too" into the negative: "Nobody has unlocked the safe ____, and the guard hasn't arrived ____."
steps.questionPrompt: Type the two negative polarity words separated by ' / ' ('already → ?', 'too → ?'):
steps.sentenceTemplate: Nobody has unlocked the safe ________, and the guard hasn't arrived ________.
steps.hint: In negatives, 'already' shifts to 'y _ _' and 'too' shifts to 'e _ _ _ _ _'!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Vaani: "Exact polarity shift! 'Already → yet' and 'too → either' sound completely natural in negatives."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Remember the negative twins: already → yet; too/also → either.
steps.simplerExample: I haven't finished yet, and my brother hasn't either.

steps.subtopicTitle: Auxiliary Inversion, Subject Wh-Questions & Question Tags
steps.memoryAidLabel: Memory Aid (Peculiar Definition — Not a Formal Rule)
steps.peculiarDefinition: In ordinary questions, the First Auxiliary jumps in front of the Subject like a polite escort ('Are you coming?', 'Where did she go?'). EXCEPT when 'Who / What / Which' IS the Subject—then it already stands in front, so NO 'do/does/did' jumps in ('Who rang the bell?')!
steps.formalDefinition: Interrogatives fall into Yes/No questions (Aux1 + Subject + Main Verb), Wh-questions (Wh-word + Aux1 + Subject + Main Verb, unless the Wh-word itself is the subject), Alternative questions, and Question Tags (short inverted auxiliary + pronoun tags reversing the statement's polarity).
steps.simpleExplanation:
Lock down three high-scoring interrogative patterns:
1) Yes/No & Object Wh-Questions: Move ONLY the first auxiliary before the subject ('Have the witnesses arrived?', 'Why did she leave early?'). Keep indirect/embedded questions in STATEMENT order ('Tell me where she went', NOT *where did she go!).
2) Subject Wh-Questions (NO do-support!): Compare 'Who broke the window?' (Subject = Who → NO 'did') vs. 'Who(m) did you see?' (Object = Who → needs 'did').
3) Question Tags: Positive statement → Negative tag ('She sings well, doesn't she?'); Negative statement (including 'hardly, seldom, never, nobody') → Positive tag ('He seldom arrives late, does he?'). Special tags: 'I am right, AREN'T I?', 'Let's start, SHALL we?', imperatives 'Open the door, WILL you?', and 'Everyone clapped, DIDN'T THEY?' ('nobody/everyone' takes 'they'!).

structurePatterns.formula: Object Wh: Wh + do/does/did + Subject + V1 | Subject Wh: Who/What + Finite Verb
structurePatterns.sample: What did Chikoo find? (Object) vs. What caused the noise? (Subject — NO 'did')

structurePatterns.formula: Statement (+), Aux n't + Pronoun? | Statement (-), Aux + Pronoun?
structurePatterns.sample: I am invited, aren't I? • Let's go, shall we? • Nobody called, did they?

realLifeExamples.sentence: Who unlocked the storeroom, and whom did the watchman question afterwards?
realLifeExamples.contextNote: 'Who unlocked' = Subject Wh-question (no 'did'); 'whom did the watchman question' = Object Wh-question (uses 'did').

realLifeExamples.sentence: Everyone remembered the password, didn't they?
realLifeExamples.contextNote: Indefinite 'Everyone' takes plural pronoun 'they' in the question tag.

correctVsIncorrect.incorrectSentence: Where you kept the spare key, and I am on time, amn't I?
correctVsIncorrect.correctSentence: Where did you keep the spare key, and I am on time, aren't I?
correctVsIncorrect.whyItHappens: Direct Wh-questions require auxiliary inversion ('did you keep'), and the standard negative tag for 'I am' is 'aren't I?' (never *amn't I).

exceptions: Negative Yes/No questions express surprise or seek confirmation: 'Didn't you hear the announcement?' (expected answer 'Yes, I did' or 'No, I didn't' depending on facts—always answer 'Yes' if true, 'No' if false!).

steps.storyPrompt: Acharya Vidyadhar helps Chikoo reassemble a proper detective question for the suspect.
steps.questionPrompt: Tap the tiles in order to form a grammatical Wh-question:
acceptedAnswers: Why did you leave the office early?
steps.hint: Follow: Wh-word ('Why') → Auxiliary ('did') → Subject ('you') → Bare V1 ('leave') → Object ('the office') → Adverb ('early?').
steps.feedbackCorrect: Acharya Vidyadhar: "Crisp interrogation! Wh-word + 'did' + Subject + Bare V1 keeps every question razor-sharp."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Place 'did' right after 'Why' and before 'you', followed by base verb 'leave'.
steps.simplerExample: When did the train reach the station?

steps.stepTitle: Checkpoint 4: Pick the Exact Question Tag
steps.storyPrompt: Maharaj Vakya challenges you with a classic exam pair: "Nobody noticed the loose hinge, ____? And I am helpful, ____?"
steps.questionPrompt: Choose the option with BOTH accurate question tags:
options: didn't they / amn't I
did they / aren't I
did he / isn't I
didn't nobody / aren't I
steps.hint: 'Nobody' is ALREADY negative (so tag is POSITIVE) and takes 'they'; positive 'I am' takes the irregular negative tag 'aren't I?'!
steps.feedbackCorrect: Maharaj Vakya: "Royally solved! 'Nobody..., did they?' (positive + plural pronoun) and 'I am..., aren't I?' are exam classics."
steps.feedbackWrongDefault: Notice 'Nobody' makes the first statement negative (requiring positive 'did they?'), and 'I am' pairs with 'aren't I?'.

feedbackWrongByOption.didn't they / amn't I: 'Nobody' is negative so the tag must be positive ('did they'), and *amn't I is non-standard!

steps.simplerExample: Nothing went wrong, did it? / I am next, aren't I?

steps.stepTitle: Scene 2: Truth Revealed by Clean Questions!
steps.settingDescription: With crisp, unmistakable questions and zero double negatives, Detective Ira verifies that the watchman simply moved the ledger for cleaning.

dialogues.line: One clean question—'Who took the ledger to the dusting room?'—solved the whole mystery in two minutes!

summaryRules.heading: Do-Support in Negatives & Questions
summaryRules.ruleSummary: When no auxiliary is present, insert do/does/did and restore the main verb to base V1. When auxiliaries already exist, place 'not' after the first auxiliary (or move it before the subject in questions).
summaryRules.formulaOrPattern: did not + Bare V1 (NEVER *didn't went) | Wh-word + Aux1 + Subject + Main Verb
summaryRules.example: She didn't lock the drawer. / Why did she leave early?

summaryRules.heading: Single Negative & Polarity Words
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Never combine not/n't with nothing, nobody, never, hardly, or seldom. Shift some → any, already → yet, and too → either in negatives.
summaryRules.formulaOrPattern: didn't see anyone (≡ saw nobody) | hasn't arrived yet | doesn't know either
summaryRules.example: He hardly spoke to anyone during the trip.

summaryRules.heading: Subject Wh-Questions & Special Question Tags
summaryRules.ruleSummary: Do NOT insert 'do/does/did' when Who/What/Which is the Subject ('Who called?'). Reverse polarity for Question Tags: 'I am..., aren't I?', 'Let's..., shall we?', 'Nobody..., did they?'.
summaryRules.formulaOrPattern: Subject Wh: Who + Verb (no 'do') | Negative statement ('never/nobody/little') → Positive Tag
summaryRules.example: Few students forgot the rule, did they?

memoryAids: Emergency Generator: 'Do/Does/Did' carries the tense and '-s' for negatives/questions, so the main verb relaxes back to bare V1!
Subject-Wh shortcut: 'Who broke it?' needs NO 'did' because 'Who' IS the doer!

commonMistakes.incorrectSentence: Did you saw where did he go? I didn't told nobody.
commonMistakes.correctSentence: Did you see where he went? I didn't tell anybody (or I told nobody).
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Keep V1 ('see') after 'Did', keep embedded questions in statement order ('where he went'), and avoid double negatives.

commonMistakes.incorrectSentence: Let's check the clues, will we? Everyone is ready, isn't he?
commonMistakes.correctSentence: Let's check the clues, shall we? Everyone is ready, aren't they?
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: 'Let's' takes 'shall we?', and indefinite 'everyone/everybody/nobody' takes plural 'they' in tags.

exceptions: Note the tag difference: 'A few students attended, didn't they?' (positive statement → negative tag) vs. 'Few students attended, did they?' (bare 'few' is negative → positive tag!).
textbookNotes: Grounded in Odisha Class IX Ch. 11 (Negatives and Interrogatives): auxiliary inversion, do-support, negative polarity, and question formation.

questions.questionText: Choose the grammatically accurate negative of "Meera knew the shortcut":
options: Meera did not knew the shortcut.
Meera did not know the shortcut.
Meera not knew the shortcut.
Meera does not knew the shortcut.
questions.explanation: Simple past 'knew' inserts 'did not' and returns the main verb to base V1 ('know').
questions.grammarRule: After 'do/does/did', always use the bare base verb (V1).

questions.questionText: Select the sentence FREE from a double negative:
options: We didn't see nobody near the boathouse.
She never goes nowhere without her sketchbook.
Nobody offered any objection to the new timetable.
He hadn't hardly finished dinner when the bell rang.
questions.explanation: 'Nobody' (single negative) pairs cleanly with 'any' (non-assertive polarity word).
questions.grammarRule: Do not combine two negative words (not, never, nobody, nothing, hardly) in one clause.

questions.questionText: Which question asks about the SUBJECT (and therefore omits 'do/does/did')?
options: Who did you invite to the science fair?
Which key opened the brass chest?
Where did the courier leave the parcel?
What does this ancient symbol mean?
questions.explanation: In 'Which key opened the brass chest?', 'Which key' IS the Subject performing 'opened', so no 'did' is inserted.
distractorRationales: 'Who' is the object ('you invited who') → needs 'did'.
questions.grammarRule: Omit do/does/did when Who/What/Which acts as the Subject of the question.

questions.questionText: Add the standard question tag: "I am scheduled to speak first, ____?"
options: amn't I
aren't I
isn't I
am I
questions.explanation: Positive 'I am' always takes the special contracted negative tag 'aren't I?' (whereas 'I am not' takes 'am I?').
distractorRationales: Positive tag cannot follow a positive statement here.
questions.grammarRule: Positive 'I am...' uses the irregular question tag 'aren't I?'.

questions.questionText: Pick the accurate tags for these two sentences: (1) "Let's review the notes, ____?" (2) "Open the eastern window, ____?"
options: will we / shall you
shall we / will you
don't we / do you
can we / aren't you
questions.explanation: 'Let's' (suggestion) takes 'shall we?'; positive imperatives take 'will you?' (or 'won't you?').
distractorRationales: Correct: 'Let's..., shall we?' and imperative '..., will you?'.
questions.grammarRule: Pair 'Let's...' with 'shall we?' and imperatives with 'will you?' / 'won't you?'.

questions.questionText: Choose the accurate question tag: "Rohan seldom misses morning assembly, ____?"
options: doesn't he
does he
isn't he
did he
questions.explanation: 'Seldom' gives the statement negative force (= almost never), so the tag must be POSITIVE ('does he?').
distractorRationales: Wrongly uses a negative tag after negative 'seldom'.
Correct: positive tag 'does he?' after semi-negative 'seldom'.
questions.grammarRule: Statements containing seldom, hardly, scarcely, rarely, little, or few take POSITIVE question tags.

options: Do you know where does the principal live?
Do you know where the principal lives?
Could you tell me what time is it?
Please explain why did the machine stop.
questions.explanation: In embedded questions ('Do you know where...'), invert ONLY the opening 'Do you know', and keep the inner clause in normal Subject + Verb statement order ('where the principal lives').
distractorRationales: Correct: statement order 'the principal lives' inside the embedded clause.
questions.grammarRule: Embedded Wh-clauses keep Subject + Verb order without auxiliary inversion.

questions.questionText: Choose the natural negative of "She has to submit the project today":
options: She hasn't to submit the project today.
She doesn't have to submit the project today.
She doesn't has to submit the project today.
She not has to submit the project today.
questions.explanation: Modal-like 'has to' (= must) forms negatives and questions with do-support: 'doesn't have to' / 'Does she have to...?'.
distractorRationales: Standard modern English uses 'doesn't have to' for obligation.
questions.grammarRule: Negate 'has/have/had to' (obligation) with 'doesn't / don't / didn't have to'.

questions.subtopicTitle: First auxiliary only moves in questions
questions.questionText: Turn "The parcel will have been delivered by noon" into a Yes/No question:
options: Will have been the parcel delivered by noon?
Will the parcel have been delivered by noon?
Does the parcel will have been delivered by noon?
Have the parcel will been delivered by noon?
questions.explanation: In multi-word verb groups ('will have been delivered'), ONLY the FIRST auxiliary ('Will') moves before the subject ('the parcel').
distractorRationales: Moves all three auxiliaries ahead of subject.
questions.grammarRule: Move only the FIRST auxiliary verb in front of the subject when forming questions.

questions.questionText: Convert "We brought some extra torches" into the negative cleanly:
options: We didn't brought any extra torches.
We didn't bring some extra torches.
We didn't bring any extra torches.
We not brought any extra torches.
questions.explanation: Change 'brought' to 'didn't bring' (base V1) and 'some' to 'any' in negative statements.
questions.grammarRule: Change 'some / something / someone' to 'any / anything / anyone' in standard negatives.

questions.subtopicTitle: A few vs Few in question tags
questions.questionText: Choose the accurate pair of question tags: (1) "A few members arrived early, ____?" (2) "Few members knew the code, ____?"
options: didn't they / didn't they
didn't they / did they
did they / didn't they
did they / did they
questions.explanation: 'A few' is positive (= some), so it takes negative tag 'didn't they?'; bare 'few' is negative (= hardly any), so it takes positive tag 'did they?'.
distractorRationales: Correct: 'A few' → negative tag; bare 'few' → positive tag.
questions.grammarRule: Pair 'a few / a little' (positive) with negative tags, and bare 'few / little' (negative) with positive tags.

questions.questionText: If Detective Ira asks "Didn't you lock the gate?" and the gate IS actually locked, what is the standard English short answer?
options: Yes, I didn't.
No, I did.
Yes, I did.
Not yes, I locked.
questions.explanation: In English, short answers match the REALITY of the action, not whether the question was phrased negatively: if you DID lock it, say 'Yes, I did' (never *Yes, I didn't).
distractorRationales: Correct: 'Yes, I did' confirms that locking occurred.
questions.grammarRule: Answer Yes/No and negative questions according to truth ('Yes + positive' if true; 'No + negative' if false).

questions.questionText: Which is the grammatically accurate negative command/request?
options: Not touch the fragile compass.
Do not touching the fragile compass.
Do not touch the fragile compass.
Doesn't touch the fragile compass.
questions.explanation: Negative imperatives always begin with 'Do not / Don't + Bare V1' (even if 'please' comes first: 'Please don't touch...').
questions.grammarRule: Form negative imperatives with 'Do not / Don't + Bare V1'.

questions.questionText: Which TWO questions are both grammatically acceptable ways to ask the same thing? (Pick the single valid option.)
options: 'Whom did you speak to?' and 'To whom did you speak?'
'To who did you speak?' and 'Whom did you speak?'
'To whom did you speak to?' and 'Who did you spoke to?'
'Who did speak to you?' and 'To whom you spoke?'
questions.explanation: Option A shows both natural stranded preposition ('Who/Whom did you speak to?') and formal fronted preposition ('To whom did you speak?').
distractorRationales: *To who uses subject case after preposition; missing 'to' in second.
Duplicates 'to' in first and puts V2 'spoke' after 'did' in second.
Changes meaning in first and omits inversion in second.
questions.grammarRule: Use 'To whom did you...' (formal) or 'Who(m) did you ... to?' (neutral).

questions.subtopicTitle: Tag pronoun for Everyone / Nobody / Something
questions.storyContext: Detective Ira closes the interrogation register.
questions.questionText: Pick the option with accurate tag pronouns for both: "Everything is ready, ____? Everyone signed the log, ____?"
options: isn't they / didn't he
isn't it / didn't they
aren't they / didn't they
isn't it / didn't it
questions.explanation: Thing indefinites ('everything, nothing, something') use 'it' in tags ('isn't it?'), whereas person indefinites ('everyone, somebody, nobody') use 'they' ('didn't they?').
questions.grammarRule: In question tags, 'everything/nothing/something' takes 'it', while 'everyone/everybody/nobody' takes 'they'.
